subject: math
title: Probability: Likelihood Words and the Probability Line
seo_title: Grade 4 Probability Worksheets: Probability Line and Likelihood (Free, with Answer Key)
standard_text: Use mathematical language, including the terms “impossible”, “unlikely”, “equally likely”, “likely”, and “certain”, to describe the likelihood of events happening, represent this likelihood on a probability line, and use it to make predictions and informed decisions
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 math worksheets on probability: describe events as impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely or certain, place them on a probability line from 0 to 1, compare spinners and bags of counters, make predictions and decide if a game is fair. 100 questions with an answer key, following the Ontario curriculum (D2.1).
key_big: Impossible is 0, certain is 1, and equally likely is halfway at 0.5.
key_sub: Likely events go between 0.5 and 1, unlikely events between 0 and 0.5. Look at the size of each part of a spinner or bag, not just the number of sections.
body_html:
The five probability words

Probability tells us how likely something is to happen. Impossible means it can never happen. Certain means it must happen. Unlikely means it could happen, but probably will not. Likely means it will probably happen. Equally likely means it is just as likely to happen as not to happen.

WordMeaningExample
impossiblecan never happenrolling a 7 on a number cube (1 to 6)
unlikelycould happen, but probably will notfinding a toonie on the sidewalk
equally likelysame chance to happen or nota coin landing on heads
likelywill probably happensnow on the ground in Winnipeg in January
certainmust happenThanksgiving in October

The probability line

A probability line goes from 0 to 1. Impossible events go at 0. Certain events go at 1. Equally likely events go halfway, at 0.5. Unlikely events go between 0 and 0.5. Likely events go between 0.5 and 1.

Example

A spinner has 10 equal sections. 7 are green. Where does landing on green go on the line?

7 of 10 equal sections is 7 tenths. Count 7 steps from 0.

Answer: 0.7, between 0.5 and 1 (likely)

Spinners and bags: look at the size of each part

A spinner is more likely to land on a colour that covers more of it. Compare the size of the parts, not just the number of sections. In a bag, the colour with more counters is more likely.

Example

Which colour is the arrow most likely to land on?

Yellow is one big section: half of the spinner. Red covers a quarter, and so does blue.

Answer: yellow

Compare likelihood

To compare two events, look at the part of the whole for each one. The event closer to 1 on the probability line is more likely.

Example

Bag A has 3 red and 1 blue counter. Bag B has 3 red and 7 blue counters. Where is red more likely?

Bag A: 3 of 4 are red, more than half. Bag B: 3 of 10 are red, less than half.

Answer: Bag A

Predictions and fair games

Use the chance to predict. If red is 1 of 4 equal sections, predict red about 1 time in every 4 spins. Real results vary a little each time. A game is fair when every player has the same chance to win.

Example

Nathan wins on an even number. Leah wins on an odd number. Is the game fair?

Even: 2, 4, 6. Odd: 1, 3, 5. Each player has 3 of the 6 faces.

Answer: Yes, it is fair

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Saying certain when it is only likelyCertain means it must happen. If it could fail, it is likely (between 0.5 and 1)
Saying impossible when it is only unlikelyIf it could happen even once, it is not impossible and does not go at 0
Counting sections, not their sizeCompare how much of the spinner each colour covers
Thinking more red counters always means more likelyLook at the whole bag: 3 of 4 is more likely than 8 of 20
Thinking a colour is “due” after it has not come upA spinner or coin does not remember: the chance stays the same

faq.q: What do Grade 4 students learn about probability in Ontario?
faq.a: In the Ontario Mathematics Curriculum (2020), expectation D2.1, Grade 4 students use the words impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely and certain, place events on a probability line from 0 to 1, and use the likelihood to make predictions and decisions.
A probability line is a number line from 0 to 1. Impossible events go at 0, certain events go at 1 and equally likely events go halfway, at 0.5.

faq.q: What is the difference between likely and certain?
faq.a: Likely means it will probably happen, but it might not, like picking red from a bag with 9 red counters and 1 blue. Certain means it must happen, like picking red from a bag with only red counters.

faq.q: How do you know if a game is fair?
faq.a: A game is fair when every player has the same chance to win. For example, one player wins on an even number and the other on an odd number: each has 3 of the 6 faces of a number cube.

items.q: Ava rolls a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. She will roll a 7. How likely is this?
items.e: The cube only has the numbers 1 to 6. There is no 7, so rolling a 7 can never happen. It is impossible.

items.q: Kai draws a triangle. It will have 4 sides. How likely is this?
items.e: Every triangle has exactly 3 sides. A triangle with 4 sides can never happen, so it is impossible.

items.q: Next month will have 45 days. How likely is this?
items.e: Every month has 28 to 31 days. A month with 45 days can never happen, so it is impossible.

items.q: The sun will rise tomorrow morning. How likely is this?
items.e: The sun rises every morning. It must happen, so it is certain.

items.q: Thanksgiving in Canada will be in October next year. How likely is this?
items.e: Canadian Thanksgiving is always on the second Monday of October. It must happen, so it is certain.

items.q: Arjun has 4 quarters in his pocket and no other coins. He takes out one coin without looking. It will be a quarter. How likely is this?
items.e: Every coin in his pocket is a quarter, so he must take out a quarter. It is certain.

items.q: On a cold, snowy day in January, Liam will wear mitts to walk to school. How likely is this?
items.e: Most children wear mitts on a cold, snowy day. But Liam could forget them, so it is likely, not certain.

items.q: A pumpkin bought at a farm market in October will be orange. How likely is this?
items.e: Most pumpkins are orange, but some are white or green. So it is likely, not certain.

items.q: In Priya’s class, 22 students like soccer and 3 do not. The teacher picks one student without looking. The student will like soccer. How likely is this?
items.e: 22 of the 25 students like soccer. That is most of the class, so it is likely. It is not certain, because 3 students do not like soccer.

items.q: Noah will find a toonie on the sidewalk on the way to school. How likely is this?
items.e: It could happen, but it almost never does. So it is unlikely. It is not impossible: people do drop coins.

items.q: There are 30 names in a hat. Chloe’s name is one of them. The teacher picks one name. It will be Chloe’s name. How likely is this?
items.e: Chloe’s name is only 1 of the 30 names. It could be picked, but probably will not be. So it is unlikely, not impossible.

items.q: A moose will walk down a busy street in downtown Toronto today. How likely is this?
items.e: Moose live in forests, far from big city streets. It has happened, but very rarely. So it is unlikely, not impossible.

items.q: Hana tosses a coin. It will land on heads. How likely is this?
items.e: A coin has 2 sides: heads and tails. Heads is just as likely to happen as not to happen, so it is equally likely.

items.q: Ethan has 2 cards face down: one red card and one black card. He picks one. It will be the red card. How likely is this?
items.e: There is 1 red card and 1 black card. Picking red and picking black have the same chance, so it is equally likely.

items.q: Owen rolls a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. He will roll an even number. How likely is this?
items.e: Even numbers: 2, 4 and 6 (3 faces). Not even: 1, 3 and 5 (3 faces). 3 and 3 are the same, so it is equally likely.

items.q: Which event is certain?
items.e: Every week has 7 days, so it must happen. The other events might happen or might not.

items.q: Which event is impossible?
c: Rolling a 6 on a number cube
Rolling a 0 on a number cube
items.e: A number cube has the numbers 1 to 6. There is no 0, so rolling a 0 can never happen. The other events can happen.

items.q: Jayden’s hockey team won its last 5 games. Jayden says, “It is certain that we will win the next game.” Which word should he use instead?
items.e: A good team will probably win, but it could still lose. If something could fail to happen, it is not certain. The better word is likely.

items.q: Leah buys 1 of the 200 tickets for the school raffle. She says, “It is impossible that I will win.” Which word should she use instead?
items.e: Leah has a ticket, so she could win. 1 of 200 is a very small chance, so the right word is unlikely, not impossible.

items.q: Which word means “it could happen, but it probably will not”?
items.e: Unlikely means it can happen, but probably will not. Impossible means it can never happen.

items.q: On a probability line from 0 to 1, where does an impossible event go?
items.e: Impossible is the lowest chance there is, so it goes at the very start: 0. Near 0 (but not at 0) is for unlikely events.

items.q: On a probability line from 0 to 1, where does a certain event go?
items.e: Certain is the highest chance there is, so it goes at the very end: 1. Near 1 (but not at 1) is for likely events.

items.q: On a probability line from 0 to 1, where does an equally likely event go?
items.e: Equally likely is halfway between impossible (0) and certain (1). Halfway is 0.5. 2 is not on the line at all.

items.q: On a probability line from 0 to 1, where does an unlikely event go?
items.e: Unlikely means it could happen, but probably will not. That is more than impossible (0) but less than equally likely (0.5).

items.q: Which word best describes the chance shown by the arrow?
items.e: The arrow is at 0.9. That is close to 1, but not at 1. So it is likely, not certain.

items.q: Which word best describes the chance shown by the arrow?
items.e: The arrow is at 0.2. That is between 0 and 0.5, closer to 0. So it is unlikely. It is not impossible, because it is not at 0.

items.q: Which word describes the chance shown by the arrow?
items.e: The arrow is at 1, the very end of the line. That means certain.

items.q: Which word describes the chance shown by the arrow?
items.e: The arrow is at 0.5, exactly halfway between 0 and 1. That means equally likely.

items.q: Which word describes the chance shown by the arrow?
items.e: The arrow is at 0, the very start of the line. That means impossible.

items.q: Which letter shows the chance of rolling a 7 on a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6?
items.e: There is no 7 on the cube, so it is impossible. Impossible goes at 0: point A.

items.q: Which letter shows the chance of a coin landing on heads?
items.e: Heads and tails are equally likely, so the chance is halfway: 0.5. That is point C.

items.q: Which letter best shows the chance of snow on the ground in Winnipeg on January 15?
items.e: Winnipeg almost always has snow on the ground in January. It is very likely, but not certain, so it goes near 1: point D.

items.q: A bag has 1 blue counter and 4 red counters. Which letter shows the chance of picking the blue counter?
items.e: 1 of the 5 counters is blue. That could happen, but probably will not: unlikely. It goes between 0 and 0.5, near 0: point B.

items.q: A spinner has 10 equal sections: 7 green and 3 yellow. Which letter shows the chance of landing on green?
items.e: 7 of the 10 equal sections are green: 7 tenths = 0.7. That is point C.

items.q: A spinner has 10 equal sections: 7 green and 3 yellow. Which letter shows the chance of landing on yellow?
items.e: 3 of the 10 equal sections are yellow: 3 tenths = 0.3. That is point B. Point C (0.7) is for green.

items.q: A spinner has 10 equal sections: 7 green and 3 yellow. Which letter shows the chance of landing on green or yellow?
items.e: Every section is green or yellow, so the arrow must land on one of them. That is certain: 1, point D.

items.q: The line is split into tenths. What number does the arrow show?
items.e: Each small step is 0.1. Count the steps from 0: 6 steps, so 0.6. 0.4 counts back from 1. 0.7 counts the tick marks instead of the steps.

items.q: A bag has 10 counters: 4 red and 6 blue. Where on the probability line does picking a red counter go?
items.e: 4 of the 10 counters are red: 4 tenths = 0.4. 0.6 is the chance of blue. 4 is not on a line that goes from 0 to 1.

items.q: The weather forecast says rain is likely on Saturday. Kai puts “rain on Saturday” at 1 on the probability line. Where should it go?
items.e: Likely means it will probably happen, but it is not sure. 1 is only for certain events. Likely goes between 0.5 and 1.

items.q: A bag has 10 counters: 1 blue and 9 red. Mei puts “picking the blue counter” at 0, because it probably will not happen. Where should it go?
items.e: There is 1 blue counter, so it can happen: it is not impossible. 1 of 10 = 1 tenth = 0.1. 0.9 is the chance of red.

sets.title: Spinners and bags: look at the size of each part

items.q: The spinner has 4 equal sections. Which colour is the arrow most likely to land on?
items.e: 3 of the 4 equal sections are red and only 1 is blue, so red is most likely. There is no green, so green is impossible.

items.q: The spinner has 10 equal sections. Landing on green is …
items.e: 9 of the 10 equal sections are green, so green is likely. It is not certain, because 1 section is yellow.

items.q: Landing on blue is …
items.e: Every section is blue. The arrow must land on blue, so it is certain.

items.q: Landing on purple is …
items.e: There is no purple section on this spinner. The arrow can never land on purple, so it is impossible.

items.q: Landing on red is …
items.e: 3 of the 6 equal sections are red and 3 are not. Red covers half of the spinner, so landing on red is equally likely.

items.q: Which colour is the arrow most likely to land on?
items.e: Do not just count sections. Look at their size. The one yellow section is half of the spinner. Red and blue each cover only a quarter.

items.q: This spinner has 3 sections. Landing on red is …
items.e: Red is only 1 of the 3 sections, but it is a big one: it covers 3 quarters of the spinner. So red is likely, not unlikely. It is not certain, because of the blue and green parts.

items.q: Amira picks one counter from the bag without looking. Which colour is she most likely to pick?
items.e: There are 6 red counters and only 2 blue counters. More red counters means red is more likely.

items.q: Picking a red counter from this bag is …
items.e: Only 1 of the 10 counters is red. It can happen, but not often, so it is unlikely, not impossible.

items.q: Picking a yellow counter from this bag is …
items.e: 5 of the 10 counters are yellow and 5 are not. Yellow and not yellow have the same chance, so it is equally likely.

items.q: Which colour is least likely to be picked?
items.e: Count each colour: red 3, blue 4, yellow 1. Yellow has the fewest counters, so it is least likely.

items.q: Put the colours in order from most likely to least likely.
items.e: Count each colour: blue 5, green 3, red 2. The most counters is most likely: blue, green, red.

items.q: Where on the probability line does picking a red counter go?
items.e: 3 of the 8 counters are red. Half of 8 is 4, and 3 is less than 4. So red is unlikely: between 0 and 0.5.

items.q: The spinner has 10 equal sections. What number on the probability line shows landing on red?
items.e: 4 of the 10 equal sections are red: 4 tenths = 0.4. 0.6 is the chance of blue. The line only goes from 0 to 1, so 4 is not on it.

items.q: Owen rolls a number cube. Rolling a number less than 3 is …
items.e: Less than 3 means 1 or 2: only 2 of the 6 faces. The other 4 faces are not less than 3. So it is unlikely, not impossible.

items.q: Owen rolls a number cube. Rolling a number greater than 0 is …
items.e: Every face shows 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6. All of them are greater than 0, so it is certain.

items.q: A spinner has 5 equal sections: 4 blue and 1 red. Aiden says landing on red is impossible, because there is only one red section. Is he right?
items.e: There is a red section, so the arrow can land on it. It is not impossible. 1 of 5 sections is a small part, so red is unlikely.

items.q: Maya colours a spinner with 6 equal sections. She wants landing on blue to be certain. How many sections should she colour blue?
items.e: Certain means it must happen, so every section must be blue: all 6. With 5 blue sections, blue is only likely.

items.q: A bag has 4 red and 4 blue counters. Which change makes picking red likely, but not certain?
items.e: With 3 more red, there are 7 red and 4 blue: red is likely. Taking out all the blue counters makes red certain, not just likely.

items.q: The spinner has 8 equal sections. Which two colours are equally likely?
items.e: Red has 4 sections, blue has 2 and yellow has 2. Blue and yellow cover the same amount, so they are equally likely.

sets.title: Compare likelihood: more, less or equally likely

items.q: On which spinner is landing on red most likely?
items.e: Compare how much of each spinner is red. C is three quarters red. D has 3 red sections, but they are small: together they are less than half of the spinner.

items.q: From which bag is picking a blue counter least likely?
items.e: Each bag has 6 counters. Bag C has only 1 blue counter, the fewest, so blue is least likely there.

items.q: On which spinner are red and blue equally likely?
items.e: On Spinner D, red and blue each cover 1 of the 4 equal sections, so they are equally likely. On B, red and blue each have 1 section, but the red section is bigger.

items.q: From which bag is picking a red counter certain?
items.e: Bag A has only red counters, so red is certain. Bag B is likely to give red, but not certain, because it has 1 blue counter.

items.q: From which bag is picking a yellow counter unlikely, but not impossible?
items.e: Bag B has 1 yellow counter out of 6: it can happen, but probably will not. Bag A has no yellow, so yellow is impossible there, not unlikely.

items.q: Bag A has 7 red and 3 blue counters. Bag B has 4 red and 6 blue counters. From which bag is picking red more likely?
items.e: Both bags have 10 counters. Bag A has 7 red, Bag B has only 4. So red is more likely from Bag A.

items.q: Bag A has 5 red and 5 blue counters. Bag B has 2 red and 8 blue counters. Which sentence is true?
c: Red is equally likely from both
Red is more likely from Bag A
Red is more likely from Bag B
Red is impossible from Bag B
items.e: Both bags have 10 counters. Bag A has 5 red (equally likely). Bag B has only 2 red (unlikely). So red is more likely from Bag A.

items.q: Bag A has 3 red and 1 blue counter. Bag B has 6 red and 2 blue counters. Which sentence is true?
c: Red is equally likely from both
Red is more likely from Bag B
Red is certain from Bag B
Red is more likely from Bag A
items.e: Bag B is just Bag A doubled: 3 red for every 1 blue. In both bags, 3 of every 4 counters are red. More red counters does not mean more likely when there are also more blue counters.

items.q: Bag A has 2 green and 2 yellow counters. Bag B has 5 green and 5 yellow counters. Which sentence is true?
c: Green is more likely from Bag A
Green is more likely from Bag B
Green is equally likely from both
Green is impossible from Bag A
items.e: In both bags, half the counters are green. So picking green is equally likely from both bags. Bag B has more green counters, but it also has more yellow ones.

items.q: Kai says picking red is more likely from Bag B (8 red, 12 blue) than from Bag A (3 red, 1 blue), because Bag B has more red counters. Is he right?
c: No, red is impossible from Bag B
No, red is more likely from Bag A
Yes, Bag B has more red
items.e: Look at the whole bag. In Bag A, 3 of 4 counters are red: likely. In Bag B, 8 of 20 are red: less than half, so unlikely. Red is more likely from Bag A.

items.q:
Which order goes from least likely to most likely?
P: rolling a 7 on a number cube (1 to 6)
Q: a coin landing on heads
R: rolling a number less than 6 on a number cube
items.e: P is impossible (0). Q is equally likely (0.5). R: 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5 is 5 of the 6 faces, so it is likely. Least to most likely: P, Q, R.

items.q: Event P is at 0.3 on the probability line. Event Q is at 0.8. Which sentence is true?
c: P is more likely than Q
Q is more likely than P
P and Q are equally likely
items.e: The closer to 1, the more likely. 0.8 is closer to 1 than 0.3, so Q is more likely. Q is not certain, because it is not at 1.

items.q: Which is more likely when you roll a number cube: rolling an even number or rolling a 6?
items.e: Even numbers are 2, 4 and 6: 3 faces. A 6 is only 1 face. 3 faces give a bigger chance, so an even number is more likely.

items.q: Which is more likely: a coin landing on heads, or a number cube landing on 1?
items.e: Heads is 1 of 2 sides: equally likely (0.5). A 1 is only 1 of 6 faces: unlikely. So heads is more likely.

items.q: A spinner has 4 equal sections and 1 is red. A bag has 2 red and 2 blue counters. Which is more likely: landing on red or picking a red counter?
items.e: Spinner: 1 of 4 sections is red, so red is unlikely. Bag: 2 of 4 counters are red, so red is equally likely. Picking a red counter is more likely.

items.q: A bag has 4 red and 4 blue counters. Compared with picking blue, picking red is …
items.e: There are 4 red and 4 blue counters: the same number. So red and blue are equally likely.

items.q: Compared with landing on red, landing on blue is …
items.e: Blue has 4 sections, but they are small. Together they cover half of the spinner. The red section covers the other half. So blue and red are equally likely.

items.q: Which event is least likely?
c: rolling a 1 on a number cube
items.e: Rolling a 1 is 1 of 6 faces: unlikely. Tails is equally likely. 3 red and 1 blue gives a likely red. 2 red and 2 blue gives an equally likely red. So rolling a 1 is least likely.

items.q: Spinner A has 10 equal sections and 3 are red. Spinner B has 10 equal sections and 6 are red. Which sentence is true?
c: Red is equally likely on both
Red is more likely on Spinner B
Red is certain on Spinner B
Red is more likely on Spinner A
items.e: Spinner A: red is 0.3 on the probability line. Spinner B: red is 0.6. 0.6 is closer to 1, so red is more likely on Spinner B.

items.q: Which is more likely: picking red from a bag with only red counters, or landing on red on a spinner that is half red?
c: landing on red on the spinner
items.e: A bag with only red counters makes red certain (1). A half red spinner makes red equally likely (0.5). Certain is more likely than equally likely.

items.q: Hana spins this spinner 40 times. About how many times should she predict red?
items.e: Red is 1 of 4 equal sections, so about 1 spin in every 4 is red. 40 ÷ 4 = 10. 30 is the prediction for blue, not red.

items.q: Lucas spins this spinner 20 times. Which result would be most surprising?
items.e: Half the spinner is red and half is blue, so you expect about 10 of each. Results near 10 are normal. Red every single time is possible, but very unlikely.

items.q: Benjamin picks a counter, looks at it and puts it back. He does this 20 times. Which prediction is best?
items.e: 3 of the 4 counters are red, so red should come up about 3 times as often as blue. Red 15 and blue 5 fits best. Red 20 is unlikely, because blue can be picked too.

items.q: Maya spins a spinner 30 times. Which colour will most likely come up on the next spin?
items.e: Red came up most often (16 times), so red probably covers the biggest part of the spinner. Yellow is never “due”: the spinner does not remember.

items.q: How many more times did red come up than yellow?
items.e: Red 16, yellow 5. How many more means subtract: 16 − 5 = 11.

items.q: Arjun tosses a coin 5 times and gets tails every time. What about the next toss?
c: Heads and tails are still equally likely
items.e: A coin does not remember what happened before. Every toss, heads and tails are equally likely.

items.q: A game is fair when …
c: each player has the same chance to win
items.e: Fair means equally likely to win. Taking turns is nice, but a game can still be unfair if one player has a bigger chance.

items.q: Zoe gets a point when the spinner lands on red. Jayden gets a point when it lands on blue. Which spinner makes the game fair?
items.e: On Spinner B, red and blue each cover half, so both players are equally likely to get a point. On C, the blue part is bigger, so Jayden would have a better chance.

items.q: Arjun and Ava roll a number cube. Arjun wins on 1 or 2. Ava wins on 3, 4, 5 or 6. Is the game fair?
c: No, Arjun is more likely to win
No, Ava is more likely to win
No, Ava is certain to win
items.e: Arjun wins on 2 faces and Ava wins on 4 faces. Ava has more ways to win, so the game is not fair. Ava is not certain to win, because a 1 or 2 can be rolled.

items.q: Nathan wins if a number cube shows an even number. Leah wins if it shows an odd number. Is the game fair?
c: No, Leah is more likely to win
No, Nathan is more likely to win
items.e: Even: 2, 4, 6. Odd: 1, 3, 5. Each player has 3 of the 6 faces, so they are equally likely to win. The game is fair.

items.q: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue counters. Owen wins on red and Emma wins on blue. How can they make the game fair?
items.e: Fair means the same number of red and blue counters. 3 + 2 = 5 blue, the same as 5 red. Adding 5 blue would give 8 blue: then Emma has the better chance.

items.q: Kai wins a prize if he picks a green counter. Bag A has 2 green and 6 yellow counters. Bag B has 6 green and 2 yellow counters. Which bag should he choose?
c: either bag, they are the same
items.e: Both bags have 8 counters. Bag B has 6 green, Bag A has only 2. Green is likely from Bag B, so Bag B is the better choice.

items.q: The forecast for Algonquin Park gives the chance of rain as 0.8 on Saturday and 0.1 on Sunday. Sofia’s family wants a dry day for their canoe trip. Which day should they choose?
c: either day, they are the same
items.e: 0.1 is close to 0, so rain on Sunday is unlikely. 0.8 is close to 1, so rain on Saturday is likely. Sunday is the better choice.

items.q: At the school fun fair, 200 raffle tickets are sold. Ethan buys 2 tickets. Ethan winning the raffle is …
items.e: Ethan has only 2 of the 200 tickets. He could win, but it is unlikely.

items.q: Priya rolls a number cube 60 times. About how many times should she predict a 6?
items.e: Each of the 6 faces is equally likely, so about 1 roll in every 6 is a 6. 60 ÷ 6 = 10. About 50 is the prediction for not getting a 6.

items.q: Benjamin picks a counter from a bag, looks at it and puts it back. He does this 20 times. He gets red 4 times and blue 16 times. Which bag did he most likely use?
items.e: Blue came up much more often than red, so the bag probably has many more blue counters. It cannot be 0 red, because then red would be impossible, and he picked red 4 times.

items.q: Mei tosses a coin 10 times. She gets 6 heads and 4 tails. Which sentence is true?
items.e: Heads and tails are equally likely, so you expect about 5 of each. Real results vary a little: 6 and 4 is close to 5 and 5.

items.q: Liam wins if the spinner lands on red. Spinner A is half red. Spinner B has 4 equal sections, and 1 is red. Which spinner should he choose?
c: either spinner, they are the same
items.e: On Spinner A, red is equally likely (0.5). On Spinner B, red is only 1 of 4 sections: unlikely. Spinner A gives Liam the better chance.

items.q: Chloe’s spinner has 10 equal sections: 7 green and 3 yellow. She spins it 100 times. About how many times should she predict green?
items.e: Green is 7 of every 10 sections, so predict about 7 green in every 10 spins. 100 spins is 10 groups of 10: 10 × 7 = 70. 30 is the prediction for yellow.

items.q: A box has 12 granola bars: 9 chocolate chip and 3 oatmeal. Leah takes one without looking. Where on the probability line does “getting chocolate chip” go?
items.e: 9 of the 12 bars are chocolate chip. Half of 12 is 6, and 9 is more than 6, so it is likely. It is not certain (1), because there are oatmeal bars too.
